chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Ali ibn Ri'ab, from Zurarah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

Charity (Sadaqah) is that which is given for the sake of God. In the time of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him), people would give gifts (Nihlah) and bestow gifts (Hibah), and it is not fitting for one who gives something to God, Exalted and Majestic, to take it back.
He said: And whatever was not given to God and for God's sake, then he may take it back, whether it was a gift (Nihlah) or a bestowal (Hibah), whether it was taken possession of or not.
And a man does not take back what he gives to his wife, nor does a woman take back what she gives to her husband, whether it was taken possession of or not.
Because God, the Exalted, says: 'And it is not permissible for you to take back from them anything you have given them.'
'But if they give up willingly to you anything of it, then take it in satisfaction and ease.'
And this ruling applies to the dowry (Sadaq) and gift (Hibah).

key_terms.الصَّدَقَةُ: Charity, specifically here distinguished as giving for God's sake
key_terms.وَيَهَبُونَ: They bestow gifts (Hibah, a general term for gift)
key_terms.يَنحَلُونَ: They give gifts (Nihlah, a type of gift)

ai.seo_question: Can a husband or wife take back a gift given to the other in Shia Islamic jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this ruling from Imam al-Sadiq (AS), distinguishing between *Sadaqah* (charity for God, irrevocable) and *Hibah* (gifts, revocable), while noting the exception for spousal gifts based on Quranic principles of dowry. This highlights the Shia jurisprudential view that gifts between spouses are treated with the permanence of charity, reinforcing the sanctity of marital exchanges. The hadith clarifies that revocability depends on whether the gift was given 'for God' or merely as a social gesture, with spousal gifts falling into the former category.
